The documentation is written: PROTOTYPE_1.md, a top-down narrative for someone who has never seen the car. It is built entirely from what is already in the repo, so every number and pin in it matches FULL_SCHEMA.md, FIRMWARE.md and the sketches as they stand today.

What it covers, in order:

- What it is and where we are. One-paragraph pitch, then a status box: prototype 1 drives under browser teleop as of today, with the milestone of all three links up on 5 September.
- The four-node idea. Why the car is split into VCU, PERC, ACT and GW, what each board owns and what it must never do, and why the MCX is a hub rather than a bus.
- The full component list. Boards, sensors, actuators, chassis, packs, and the fourteen resistors, trimpot and capacitor that make it work, each with a one-line reason.
- How it moves and how it sees. The transistor drive stage explained in plain words, the forward-only trade, the no-encoder consequence, why it whines at 2 kHz, and the front/back sonar decision.
- Protocol, power and the safety net. The message table, the three-supply star-ground layout, and the four independent stop layers plus the front guard and horn watchdog.
- Firmware map and driving instructions. Which file proves what, build and flash commands, WiFi name and the WASD keys.
- What we learned. The war stories written as lessons: the two latched ESP32s, the borrowed I2C pull-ups, the PERC wires in the wrong holes, the dead VIN pin, the one-byte probe that broke the bus, the floating echo pins.
- Limits and next steps. An honest list of what prototype 1 cannot do, and the six things prototype 2 should add.
- Document map pointing to the schema sheets, netlist, firmware guide and pinout reference.

All six changes are in PROTOTYPE_1.md, and the sections are renumbered so the document now runs 1 to 14 with no gaps.

Removed: the status section, the small-parts resistor table, the build and flash commands, and the closing sentence about the two chassis PDFs. The document map still points at the firmware guide for flashing, so nothing is orphaned.

Rewrote the power section around two packs. The 6 V pack feeds the four motors and the ESP32; the 9 V pack feeds the MCX, PERC and ACT. The buck module is gone from the parts table and the text. Two points I added because the new arrangement changes them:

- 6 V is genuinely better for the ESP32 than 9 V was. Its regulator drops about 0.3 W instead of 0.68 W, so it runs cool and the fan on it becomes margin rather than necessity.
- The motors and the ESP32 now share a pack. The ESP32 browns out below roughly 4.4 V at its input, and four motors starting pull a pack down hard. If it resets when the car lurches, that is the cause. The 470 uF beside the board is what covers its own WiFi bursts.

One thing I could not resolve and flagged in the document rather than papering over: the 9 V has no way into the MCX. The board's VIN pin is a dead end on stock hardware, and its only working pack input is a regulated 5 V into J3-10. Without the buck module there is nothing to bring 9 V down, so the document says the MCX stays on its USB cable, which is what it has been doing anyway and what keeps the console alive. It sits under its own heading in the power section and again in the limits list. Worth deciding before an untethered demo run.

I also updated the latch-up warning: the ESP32 and the MCX are on different supplies now, so they no longer come up together. Switch both packs at once, or the 6 V one on first and off last.

Section 4 reads as capability now. It opens with "The car moves like this:" and the five paragraphs lead on what the design does rather than what it lacks: each motor has its own switch, speed comes from pulsing that switch, steering comes from the difference between the two sides, the gyro closes the loop, the whine is the drive stage working. The last one is now "the transistors run cool by design, and the front guard keeps them there."

Removed: the parts-list sentence, the dated "the prototype drives" sentence, and both closing sections.

One fan, on the ESP32. The parts table, the power diagram and the power bullet all say a single 12 V fan cooling the ESP32's regulator. I fed it from the 9 V pack rather than the 6 V one the ESP32 sits on, because a 12 V fan is marginal to start at 6 V and runs about 70 % at 9 V. Worth knowing: the four transistors now have no forced air. Running they are comfortable at 100 mW in a 625 mW package, so the only exposure is the stall case, and the 25 cm front guard is what covers it.

The rear warning is documented from the code, not from a guess. I read rear_service() in distributed_ecu/led_blinky.c and wrote up the three things that make it trustworthy: it warns at 25 cm but clears at 32 so a wall on the threshold cannot flicker the display, it repeats once a second because the message line has no acknowledgement, and a silent sensor counts as clear so nothing invents an alert. The protocol table now carries the repeated message line.

While reading that code I also found a V,<ms> heartbeat going to both Arduinos every second, which both sketches parse. My protocol table had the older story where the horn line doubled as the keep-alive, so I corrected it.

The documentation is now README.md, so it is the repository front page.
